turns.text: What do you remember most vividly about your first morning waking up in Beidahuang after leaving Shanghai?

The cold was the first thing that reached me, even before I opened my eyes. In Shanghai, the air had always been damp, but this cold was sharp, thin, and endless. The room was cramped, bare except for the rough bedding and a chipped enamel basin. I remember the silence outside—no familiar street sounds, just the wind pushing against the walls. My hands shook as I dressed, fumbling with the stiff fabric of my work clothes. When I stepped outside, the sky was pale, almost colorless, and the fields stretched out in every direction, muddy and already crowded with figures moving slowly through the morning fog. The mud sucked at my shoes. I could smell the earth, strong and raw, and the breakfast—thin porridge—barely warmed my mouth. I felt smaller than I’d ever felt in Shanghai, as if the land itself was swallowing me.

It’s striking how the cold and the silence made everything feel unfamiliar and overwhelming. You mentioned the fields were already crowded with people in the fog—what did you notice about the other sent-down youth or local workers that first morning, and how did they react to newcomers like you?

Most of the other sent-down youth looked just as lost as I felt—faces pale, eyes darting, movements awkward as we tried to copy what the locals were doing. Some huddled in small groups, whispering in Shanghainese, clutching their shovels too tightly. The local workers kept their distance, glancing at us with a mix of suspicion and amusement. When one of us slipped in the mud, a few locals laughed quietly, but most just kept working, their bodies moving with a practiced rhythm that made our clumsiness stand out even more. No one offered instructions or a welcome. I remember feeling like we were being watched, measured, but not truly seen. That morning, I realized we were outsiders in every possible way.

I remember how my hands wouldn’t stop shaking—not just from cold, but from the eyes on us. The locals’ faces were weathered, their expressions closed. When I tried to greet an older woman, she barely nodded, already moving on. There was a line drawn, invisible but solid: we were city kids, soft and uncertain, and they had no patience for us slowing them down. Some of the sent-down youth tried to joke, to lighten the mood, but the laughter sounded thin, desperate. I felt every mistake—dropping a tool, stepping wrong in the mud—was being tallied. The locals worked in silence, shoulders hunched, and I realized quickly that here, words meant little. It was how you endured that mattered.

It sounds like even small interactions—like trying to greet someone—were charged with tension and distance. You mentioned that the locals worked in silence and that endurance seemed to matter more than words; was there a moment in those early days when you realized what it would take to be accepted, or at least tolerated, by them?

There was a morning when my boots split open in the mud, and I kept working anyway, feet soaked and numb. By midday, I could barely feel my toes, but I refused to stop, even when the pain made me dizzy. One of the local men watched me for a long time, his face unreadable. Later, as we rested, he tossed me a strip of old tire and gestured for me to wrap it around my boot. He didn’t say anything, just nodded once. That gesture—silent, practical—felt like a test I’d finally passed. After that, the laughter when I stumbled grew quieter, and sometimes a local would show me, wordlessly, how to hold a tool or brace against the wind. I learned that you earned a place there by not giving up, no matter how much you wanted to.

The day my hands cracked and bled from gripping the shovel, I kept digging anyway. The mud sucked at my boots, and every movement sent a jolt of pain through my palms. I could feel eyes on me, waiting for me to give up or ask for help. I didn’t. At the end of the shift, I sat down, hands shaking, blood mixing with the dirt. One of the older women sat nearby and slid me a bit of ointment, not meeting my eyes. She didn’t speak. I understood then that words wouldn’t get me anything, but stubbornness might. After that, the locals stopped looking through me and started looking at me. It wasn’t friendship, but it was a kind of acknowledgment—earned through blisters and silence.

That moment with the ointment says so much about how respect was shown in small, quiet ways. When you finally received that acknowledgment, did it change how you saw yourself or your place there, even if just a little?

It did, in a strange way. I stopped feeling like a guest who might be sent home at any moment. Instead, I started to see myself as someone who could survive there, someone who belonged to the mud and the wind, even if only on the edges. I noticed I moved differently—less hesitation, more purpose. I still missed Shanghai every day, but I stopped waiting for rescue. I began to measure my days by the work I finished, not by how much I wanted to leave. That small shift was the beginning of accepting that this was my life, at least for now.

The first time I realized I could stand the work, I felt a kind of stubborn pride. My hands were rough, my back ached, but I was still standing when others had dropped out for the day. That changed something inside me. I stopped shrinking from the locals’ eyes; I met them, even if only for a moment. I started to care less about how out of place I looked and more about whether I could finish the row I was assigned. My sense of myself changed—from someone who was sent there, to someone who could endure there. I still felt alone most days, but I knew I wasn’t invisible anymore. That mattered.

That shift from feeling invisible to being seen, even just for your endurance, seems powerful. Now that you look back, do you think that stubborn pride and ability to endure shaped how you faced challenges later in life, even after you left Beidahuang?

Absolutely. Even now, when I’m faced with something that feels impossible or humiliating, there’s a voice in me that says: you’ve survived worse. The memory of standing in that endless mud, hands bleeding, and refusing to quit became a private measure of what I could take. Sometimes, I worry it also made me too hard, too slow to ask for help, but it gave me a kind of grit that nothing else could have. I learned to keep moving forward, even if no one was watching, even if I was completely alone. That stubbornness has shaped every part of my life since.

I carry that stubbornness like a scar—sometimes it’s protection, sometimes it’s a weight. Whenever life has cornered me since, I draw on that memory of mud and pain and silence. I know I can keep going long after I want to stop, because I’ve done it before when nobody cared if I made it or not. But there’s a cost to it. I find it hard to trust that anyone will step in if I falter. I expect to stand alone. That’s the piece I brought with me from Beidahuang—endurance, but also a kind of distance from others. Some days I wonder if it’s strength, or just another way to survive.

Your honesty about both the strength and the loneliness that came from those years makes me think about how much we inherit from hardship, for better or worse. If you could speak to your younger self on that first cold morning in Beidahuang, knowing everything you know now, what would you want to say to them?
